Budget Like A Queen: Build Your Wealth

A free, ebook-length teaching guide to budgeting from zero: find your real numbers, choose a style that fits you, build a system with guilt-free spending, an emergency fund and a debt plan, earn more, and learn the basics of building wealth, with scripts, scam warnings and a one-page plan.

Come and sit beside me, love, and let us talk about money the way a big sister would: calmly, plainly and without any shame. If you have ever opened your banking app, felt your stomach drop and closed it again, you are in very good company. Nobody was born knowing how to handle money, and almost nobody was taught.

This guide is a complete, from-zero lesson in budgeting and building wealth. I will explain every word. I will show you every step. And I will not tell you to "just stop buying coffee," because that is lazy advice and it does not work.

A few honest promises before we begin.

I am not a financial adviser, tax adviser or lawyer. I am teaching you general ideas, not personal advice. Money rules, taxes, banks, savings products and investment options differ widely from country to country and change over time, so please check your own country's rules and, for big decisions, speak with a qualified professional.

I will not promise you riches, and I will not tell you that a budget makes money appear. What a budget does is show you where your money is already going, so that you can steer it toward the life you actually want. That alone changes a great deal.

And I will not ask you to live like a monk. A budget that has no room for joy gets abandoned in three weeks. We are building one you can live inside.

Here is what you will learn in this guide:

  • What a budget really is, and why most budgets quietly fail.
  • How to find your real numbers, even if your income changes every month.
  • Several budgeting styles, and how to pick the one that fits your personality.
  • Simple tools, from a notebook to a free app, and how to set them up.
  • How to build a system around needs, goals and guilt-free spending.
  • How to build an emergency fund without feeling deprived.
  • How to deal with debt calmly.
  • How to start growing wealth, in plain language, with honest warnings.
  • How to earn more, negotiate and protect yourself from scams.
  • A troubleshooting table, a ninety-day plan, twelve questions, a checklist and a one-page plan.

Do not try to do everything in one weekend. Read a chapter, do the small job for that chapter, and come back. Slow and steady is the whole method.

A budget is not a cage. It is a plan for your money to follow your life.

1What A Budget Really Is

Let us begin at the very beginning, as if I were teaching a child, because the basics matter more than the clever tricks.

Money comes in and money goes out. The money that comes in is called income. That might be your salary, your business earnings, side-hustle payments, allowances or help from family. The money that goes out is called expenses. That is rent, food, transport, data, school fees, clothes, treats, loan repayments and everything else.

A budget is simply a plan that says, "This is the money I expect to come in, and this is where I have decided it will go." That is all. It is not a punishment, a diet or a test of your character. It is a plan.

Think of a budget like a map for a journey. You would not drive across a big country without looking at a map, and yet many of us spend years crossing our financial lives with no map at all, then wonder why we are lost.

The three questions a budget answers

1. Where is my money going? (Many people honestly do not know.) 2. Is it going where I want it to go? (Often the answer is "not quite.") 3. What can I do differently, starting this month? (Small, realistic changes.)

What a budget is not

  • It is not a promise never to enjoy yourself.
  • It is not a measure of how good or bad you are with money.
  • It is not something you set once and forget. It is a living plan you adjust.
  • It is not only for people who earn little. People with high incomes who never plan their money often end up just as stressed.

A few words you will see in this guide

WordWhat it means
IncomeMoney coming in
ExpensesMoney going out
Fixed expensesCosts that are the same each month, such as rent
Variable expensesCosts that change, such as food or transport
SavingsMoney you set aside for later
Emergency fundSavings kept for unexpected problems
DebtMoney you owe to someone
InterestA fee for borrowing money, or a reward for saving it
Net incomeWhat you actually receive after deductions
Net worthEverything you own minus everything you owe

Do not memorise this table. Come back to it whenever a word feels fuzzy.

Big Sis Note 💖 Big Sis Note: If money has felt scary, that is not because you are bad at it. It is because nobody showed you the map. Today, you are getting the map.

2Why Most Budgets Fail (And How Yours Will Not)

Most people have tried to budget at least once. Most of them stopped. Here is why, and what we will do differently.

Failure reason one: too strict

The first budget most people make is a heroic one. Every naira, dollar or pound is assigned. No treats. No flexibility. It lasts ten days, until a friend's birthday arrives, and then it collapses and the person decides, "I am just bad at this."

What we will do instead: build in a guilt-free spending amount and a small buffer for surprises.

Failure reason two: too complicated

Spreadsheets with thirty categories, colour codes and formulas look impressive, but if tracking takes an hour a day, you will quit.

What we will do instead: start with a handful of categories and a system that takes minutes, not hours.

Failure reason three: built on guesses

Many budgets are based on what people think they spend, not what they actually spend. The two numbers are rarely the same.

What we will do instead: start with your real numbers from the last one to three months.

Failure reason four: no goals

A budget with no purpose feels like pure restriction. "Why am I saying no to everything?" A budget with a goal feels like a plan. "I am saying no to this because I am saying yes to that."

What we will do instead: attach every budget to a few clear goals you actually care about.

Failure reason five: ignoring irregular costs

School fees, annual subscriptions, festive seasons, car repairs and birthdays do not arrive monthly, but they do arrive. If your budget has no place for them, every one of them feels like an emergency.

What we will do instead: create "sinking funds," small amounts set aside for known future costs.

Failure reason six: going it alone and in secret

Money shame makes people hide their numbers from partners, family and even themselves. Hidden numbers cannot be managed.

What we will do instead: look at the numbers together with yourself first, and, where it is safe and sensible, with the people who share your money.

Common Mistake 🚨 Common Mistake: Making a "perfect" budget and then giving up the first time it is off by a little. A budget that is wrong by ten percent and followed is far better than a perfect one that is abandoned.

Take Chioma, a made-up example, who earns a steady salary. Her first budget had thirty-two categories and no room for fun. She quit in two weeks and spent a month feeling guilty. Her second attempt had six categories, a small "enjoy it" amount and one savings goal. She kept it for a year. Same woman, same income, a very different design.

3Find Your Real Numbers

This chapter is the foundation. Do not skip it, even though it is not glamorous. You cannot steer a car if you do not know where it is.

Step one: gather your records

Collect the last one to three months of your money information:

  • Bank or mobile money statements
  • Receipts, if you keep them
  • Notes of cash you spent
  • Loan or instalment statements
  • Your payslip or records of your earnings

If you do not have records, do not panic. For the next thirty days, write down everything you spend, even small things. Cash that disappears is the most common leak, so noting it, even roughly, teaches you a lot.

Step two: list your income

Write down every source of money that came in, with the date and amount. Use net income, the amount you actually received after any deductions, not the amount before.

If your income is steady, this is easy. If it changes from month to month, we will handle that in the next chapter.

Step three: list your expenses

Go through your records and sort each expense into a category. A simple starter list:

1. Housing (rent, utilities) 2. Food and groceries 3. Transport 4. Data, phone and internet 5. Family support and giving 6. Education or work costs 7. Health 8. Debt repayments 9. Personal care and clothes 10. Fun and treats 11. Savings and goals 12. Everything else

Do not worry if some things do not fit perfectly. Pick the nearest category and move on.

Step four: separate fixed from variable

  • Fixed: rent, school fees, loan repayments, subscriptions
  • Variable: food, transport, treats, clothes

Fixed costs are harder to change quickly. Variable costs are where you usually have the most room to adjust.

Step five: do the simple sums

1. Add up all your income for the month. 2. Add up all your expenses for the month. 3. Subtract expenses from income.

If the answer is positive, you have money left over. If it is zero, you are living right on the edge. If it is negative, you are spending more than you earn, which means you are either using savings or borrowing. Please do not feel shame about a negative. It is information, and the point of this whole guide is to help you change it.

A worked example (made up)

Take Amara, a made-up example, who earns 300,000 a month in her local currency. Her records show:

CategoryMonthly amount
Rent and utilities90,000
Food60,000
Transport35,000
Data and phone10,000
Family support30,000
Debt repayment25,000
Personal care and clothes20,000
Fun and treats25,000
Savings0
Unknown or forgotten15,000
Total310,000

Amara is spending 310,000 on an income of 300,000. She is 10,000 short each month, and she did not know it. Notice the "unknown or forgotten" line: those small leaks add up. This is not a character flaw. It is exactly what most people find when they look for the first time, and it is the beginning of control.

The numbers in this example are invented, for teaching only. Your own figures will be different, and that is perfectly fine.

Tiny Win ✨ Tiny Win: Finding your real numbers is the hardest part of budgeting, and you just learned how to do it. Everything after this is easier.

4If Your Income Is Irregular

If you are a freelancer, a business owner, a commission earner or anyone whose income changes month to month, a normal budget can feel impossible. Here is how to handle it.

The "baseline month" method

1. Look at the last six to twelve months of income, if you have them. 2. Find your lowest month and your average month. 3. Build your budget around your lowest month, or something close to it. 4. When you earn more than your baseline, treat the extra as a bonus and give it jobs.

This turns an unpredictable income into a predictable plan.

Give your bonus months jobs

When extra money arrives, decide quickly where it goes, before it disappears. For example:

  • Fifty percent to your buffer or emergency fund
  • Twenty percent to debt or goals
  • Twenty percent to expected future costs
  • Ten percent to enjoy guilt-free

You can set your own percentages. The point is that extra money has a plan.

Pay yourself a "salary"

Many freelancers do well by sending all their income into one account and then paying themselves a fixed amount into a separate personal account each month, like a salary. In good months, extra stays in the business account as a buffer. In slow months, the buffer tops up your salary. This smooths out the ups and downs.

Remember tax and business costs

If you earn from freelancing or a business, some of that money may need to go to tax or business costs. I am not a tax adviser, and the rules differ everywhere, so please check what applies to you. A simple habit is to set aside a percentage of every payment as soon as it arrives, in a separate place, so it is never tempting.

Take Funmi, a made-up example, a freelance designer whose income ranges widely. She looks at her last six months, finds her lowest was 120,000 and her average was 180,000, and decides to build her budget on 120,000. In a month she earns 220,000, she puts 100,000 toward her buffer. When a slow month comes, the buffer covers the gap, and she does not panic. Her income did not become steady. Her plan did.

5Choose A Budgeting Style That Fits Your Personality

There is no single "correct" way to budget. There are several, and each suits a different kind of person. Let me teach you the main ones, then help you choose.

Style one: the percentage method (often called 50/30/20)

You split your income into three buckets:

  • About fifty percent for needs: rent, food, transport, utilities, minimum debt payments.
  • About thirty percent for wants: fun, treats, eating out, hobbies.
  • About twenty percent for savings and debt: emergency fund, goals, extra debt payments.

These percentages are a starting guide, not a law. In some places, rent alone takes more than half of someone's income. If your needs cost sixty or seventy percent, that is real, and you adjust the shape: perhaps forty-five percent needs would be a dream, so you aim for ten percent savings today and grow it.

Best for: people who want something simple and flexible and do not enjoy tracking every small purchase.

Style two: the zero-based method

You give every unit of your income a job, until income minus planned spending equals zero. That does not mean you spend everything. Savings and debt repayments are jobs too. It simply means no money is left "floating" without a purpose.

Best for: people who like detail, who tend to lose track of leftovers, or who want to feel fully in control.

Style three: the envelope method

You divide cash (or digital "envelopes" in an app) into categories for the month. When the money in an envelope runs out, you stop spending in that category until the next month.

Best for: people who overspend in a few particular categories, such as food delivery or clothes, and who are helped by a physical limit.

Style four: pay yourself first

On the day your money arrives, you move savings first, then live on the rest. You do not track every small expense. You simply decide a savings amount, automate it and spend the remainder freely.

Best for: people who hate detailed tracking but are good at living within a limit, and people who struggle to save "what is left over" because nothing ever is.

Style five: the "number" method

You calculate how much you can spend freely each day or week after all your essentials and savings, and you track only that one number.

Best for: people who find categories overwhelming and want one simple limit.

A comparison table

StyleEffortControlFlexibilityGood for
Percentages (50/30/20)LowMediumHighBeginners
Zero-basedHighVery highMediumDetail lovers
EnvelopesMediumHighLowOverspenders
Pay yourself firstVery lowMediumHighAnti-trackers
One daily or weekly numberLowMediumHighSimple lovers

How to choose

Ask yourself three questions:

1. Do I enjoy details, or do they exhaust me? Detail lovers, try zero-based. Detail-haters, try pay-yourself-first or percentages. 2. Where do I usually lose money? One or two categories? Try envelopes. Everywhere? Try zero-based. 3. What will I do on a tired Tuesday? Pick the system you would still keep on your worst day.

You can mix styles. Many people do pay-yourself-first plus a weekly spending number. You can also change styles later. Nothing is permanent.

Coffee Break ☕ Coffee Break: If you are stuck choosing, start with percentages for one month. It is the gentlest on-ramp. After one month, you will know what to change.

Take Nneka, a made-up example, who hates detail. She chooses pay-yourself-first: the day her salary arrives, a fixed amount moves automatically to savings and another to her rent account. She then spends the rest freely and checks her balance once a week. It is not fancy, and it has worked for her for two years.

6Tools: From A Notebook To A Free App

Tools make budgeting easier, but they are not magic. The best tool is the one you will actually open.

Option one: a notebook

A simple notebook with income on one page and spending categories on another is a perfectly good tool. It is slow and personal, and many people find that writing things down by hand makes them more aware.

Option two: a spreadsheet

A free spreadsheet can total your categories automatically. A very simple layout:

CategoryPlannedActualDifference
Rent and utilities
Food
Transport
Data and phone
Savings
Fun

At the end of each week, update the "Actual" column. The "Difference" column shows where you are over or under.

Option three: a budgeting app

Many apps track your spending, categorise it and show charts. Some connect directly to your bank, depending on your country. Before using any app:

  • Check what it does with your data, and read its privacy policy.
  • Check whether it is available in your country and currency.
  • Check whether it is free, and what the paid version adds.
  • Never share your banking passwords with a tool you do not fully trust. Prefer apps that use official, secure connections, and remember that features and rules change, so check current platform rules.

Option four: your bank's own tools

Many banks and mobile money services show monthly spending summaries and let you create separate "pots" or sub-accounts for savings goals. These can be the simplest way to automate your plan.

Our free tool

You can also use the free Personal Budget Planner on this site to lay out your numbers.

The five-minute weekly money date

Whichever tool you use, build a tiny habit: once a week, set a timer for ten minutes with a cup of tea and do these four things:

1. Check your balance. 2. Update your spending. 3. Look at your categories: are any running out? 4. Decide one small adjustment for the coming week.

A short weekly check-in is far more effective than a long monthly panic.

Keep your money information safe

  • Use strong, unique passwords and two-step verification on banking and money apps.
  • Never share one-time codes, PINs or passwords with anyone, including people claiming to be from your bank.
  • Do not do banking on public Wi-Fi.
  • Keep your phone updated and locked.

7Build Your System: Needs, Goals And Guilt-Free Spending

Now we build your actual plan. I will give you a simple structure with four parts. You can adapt the names, but keep the shape.

Part one: needs

Your needs are the things you must pay to live and work: shelter, basic food, transport to work or school, utilities, essential data, health costs, minimum debt payments and any dependants you are responsible for.

Calculate the real monthly total. If it is much higher than expected, we will look at ways to reduce it in a later chapter.

Part two: goals

Your goals are what your money is working toward. Common ones:

  • An emergency fund
  • Paying off a debt
  • A big purchase, like a laptop or a course
  • A move, a wedding, a holiday or school fees
  • Starting a business or investing

Write each goal with an amount and a date, for example: "Emergency fund of three months' expenses by next December." A goal with a number and a date is a plan. A goal without them is a wish.

To work out a monthly amount, divide the total by the number of months. If a laptop costs 360,000 and you want it in twelve months, you need to set aside 30,000 a month.

Part three: guilt-free spending

This is the part most budgets forget, and it is what makes yours survive. Guilt-free spending is an amount each month that you can spend on anything you like, without justification, tracking or shame.

It might be 5 percent of your income. It might be 15. Choose an amount that feels like breathing room. When it is gone, it is gone, but while you have it, you enjoy it.

Why does this work? Because humans need pleasure, and a plan that bans all pleasure builds up pressure until it explodes in a big, guilty overspend. A small, guilt-free amount lets the pressure out safely.

Hot Girl Reminder 💅 Hot Girl Reminder: Enjoying your own money, within your plan, is not a betrayal of your goals. It is part of the plan.

Part four: the buffer

Add a small buffer category, perhaps three to five percent of your income, for small, unplanned costs: a cracked phone screen, a last-minute gift, a bus fare that doubled. Without a buffer, every surprise feels like a disaster and breaks your budget. With one, it is just a Tuesday.

A sample structure (made up)

Take Sade, a made-up example, who earns 250,000 a month.

PartAmountShare
Needs140,00056%
Goals (emergency fund, laptop)45,00018%
Debt beyond the minimum15,0006%
Guilt-free spending35,00014%
Buffer15,0006%
Total250,000100%

Sade's needs are higher than a textbook would suggest, and that is fine. She works with her real numbers, not an ideal. Her plan covers needs, builds a future and still leaves room for joy.

Sinking funds: for the costs that are not monthly

A sinking fund is a small amount you set aside each month for a known future cost. Examples:

  • Festive season spending
  • Annual insurance or subscriptions
  • School fees or exam fees
  • Car or phone repairs
  • Birthdays and weddings
  • Medical check-ups

Estimate the total for the year, divide by twelve and save that amount monthly in a separate place. When the cost arrives, the money is already there. This single trick removes most "financial emergencies" that were never really emergencies, just unplanned certainties.

Where to keep each pot

Keep your categories separate if you can, perhaps using different accounts, sub-accounts or labelled pots. When all your money sits in one place, it is easy to spend your savings by accident. Separate, clearly named pots protect you from yourself.

8Cut Costs Without Feeling Deprived

Most budget advice about cutting costs is either insulting ("make coffee at home!") or impossible. Let me give you a better approach.

Start with the big three

For most people, the biggest costs are housing, transport and food. Trimming ten percent from one of these often beats cutting twenty tiny things.

  • Housing: Can you negotiate rent, share costs, move at renewal or reduce utility bills? Do not make a rushed move without thinking it through.
  • Transport: Are there cheaper routes, shared rides or schedules that reduce trips?
  • Food: Planning meals, buying staples in bulk when it is cheaper and reducing waste can help a lot.

Look for leaks

A leak is a small, regular cost that you barely notice and would not miss. Examples:

  • Subscriptions you forgot about
  • Bank charges you could avoid
  • Data plans larger than you use
  • Delivery fees for things you could collect
  • Impulse purchases made when bored or sad

Go through your last two months of records and circle every recurring charge. Ask: "Do I still use this? Would I buy it again today?" Cancel what fails the test.

The twenty-four-hour rule

For any non-essential purchase above an amount you choose, wait twenty-four hours before buying. Often the desire fades. If it does not, you buy it with a clear head.

Spend on what you value, cut what you do not

This is called values-based spending. Ask: "What do I truly love spending money on?" Perhaps it is food with friends, or fashion, or travel. Then ask: "What do I spend on out of habit that I barely enjoy?" Cut the second list ruthlessly, and spend on the first list without guilt. You do not need to cut everything, only what does not make your life better.

Do not cut where it hurts your future

Do not cut essential health costs, skills you are building or necessary safety. Saving money by neglecting your health or income-building tools is expensive in the long run.

Beware of "cheap" that costs more

A very cheap item that breaks quickly can cost more than a sturdier one. A free-looking offer that hides fees can cost more than a fair price. Always look at the full cost, not just the label.

Common Mistake 🚨 Common Mistake: Cutting everything fun in the first week. Cut the leaks first, keep the joy and adjust slowly.

9Emotional Spending And Money Habits

Money is never only about maths. It is tied up with emotion, family, culture and history. Let me teach you about the feelings that quietly steer our spending.

Why we overspend

  • To soothe stress or sadness. A purchase gives a small lift of pleasure.
  • To fit in. Social pressure to keep up with friends or social media.
  • To celebrate or reward ourselves. "I deserve this" can become a daily excuse.
  • Out of boredom. Scrolling and shopping often travel together.
  • Because of habit. Always buying the same things at the same times.

None of these makes you a bad person. They make you human. The goal is not to remove emotion but to notice it.

The pause-and-ask technique

Before buying something non-essential, ask three quick questions:

1. What am I feeling right now? 2. What do I actually need? 3. Will I still want this in a week?

Just the pause can change your decision.

Social media and spending

Social media shows other people's best moments, and often their sponsored ones. If your feed makes you want things you do not need, you can mute accounts, unfollow, delete shopping apps or remove saved card details. Make impulse spending slightly harder, and it happens less.

Money and family expectations

In many families and communities, there are expectations to support relatives, give at events or help others. These can be loving and also heavy. Plan for them openly by creating a giving and family category in your budget, with a fixed amount. This lets you give generously without wrecking your own stability.

You are also allowed to say, kindly, "I cannot give that this month." Having a planned amount makes saying no less painful, because it is not about love. It is about limits.

A kind script: "I would love to help and I wish I could do more. This month I can contribute [amount]. I hope that helps."

Money shame

If you carry shame about debt, overspending or earning less than others, you are not alone. Shame keeps people hiding from their numbers, which keeps them stuck. Treat your past mistakes like a lesson, not a verdict. Everyone who has become good with money began by being confused about it.

10Build An Emergency Fund Without Feeling Deprived

An emergency fund is money set aside for real, unexpected problems: a sudden medical cost, a job loss, an urgent repair, a family emergency. It is the single most protective thing in a personal budget. Without one, every shock becomes debt. With one, a shock is a bad day instead of a disaster.

How much do you need?

A common guideline is three to six months of essential expenses, meaning your needs, not your whole lifestyle. If your needs cost 140,000 a month, three months is 420,000.

That number can feel enormous, so do not start there. Use stages:

StageTargetWhat it protects you from
StarterOne small, fixed amount, such as one week of needsA small shock without borrowing
MiniOne month of needsA short gap in income
SolidThree months of needsA job change or longer problem
StrongSix months of needsBigger shocks, or irregular income

If your income is irregular or you have dependants, aim higher over time. These are general ideas, not personal advice, and your situation may need more or less.

Where to keep it

  • Somewhere safe and easy to reach in a real emergency, but not so easy that you dip into it for a sale.
  • Separate from your everyday spending account.
  • Ideally earning at least a little interest, if your country offers safe savings options. Check current rules, fees and protections where you live.

Do not put your emergency fund into risky investments. Its job is to be there, not to grow fast.

How to build it without feeling poor

1. Start tiny and automate. Even a small amount moved on payday builds a habit. 2. Use windfalls. A bonus, tax refund, gift or extra payment can go partly to the fund. 3. Name the pot. Call it something kind, like "Peace of Mind." You will feel differently about it. 4. Celebrate each stage. Reaching your first month of needs deserves a small, free celebration. 5. Grow it in the background. Raise the amount slightly whenever your income or expenses improve.

What counts as an emergency?

Be clear with yourself in advance. A real emergency is unexpected, urgent and necessary. A sale, a holiday and a friend's party are not emergencies, however loud they feel. Write your own short list now, so you are not deciding in the heat of the moment.

What to do after using it

If you use your emergency fund, you have not failed. That is what it is for. Simply rebuild it, step by step, and be proud that you were prepared.

Take Bola, a made-up example, who earns a modest salary. She cannot save much, so she starts with 5,000 a week, automatically. In a year she has a little more than 260,000. When her phone breaks and her landlord needs an urgent payment in the same month, she covers both from her fund instead of borrowing. She was not rich. She was prepared.

11Deal With Debt Calmly

Debt is money you owe. It can be a bank loan, a credit card, a store account, a loan app or money borrowed from friends or family. Debt is not automatically evil, and it is also not harmless. The key is understanding what it costs and having a plan.

First, know exactly what you owe

Write a list with, for each debt:

DebtWho you oweAmount owedInterest rateMinimum paymentDue date

Many people avoid doing this because it hurts. But a clear list is far less scary than a vague fear. If you are unsure of an interest rate, check your statement or ask the lender.

Always pay the minimums

Missing payments can lead to fees, higher interest and damage to your ability to borrow later, depending on your country. Make sure every minimum payment is in your budget as a need.

Two simple payoff methods

When you have extra money to throw at debt, you can use one of two popular methods.

  • The snowball method: pay minimums on everything, then put all extra money toward the smallest debt. When it is gone, roll that payment into the next smallest. This gives quick wins and builds motivation.
  • The avalanche method: pay minimums on everything, then put all extra money toward the debt with the highest interest rate. This usually costs the least money over time.

Which is better? The avalanche is mathematically cheaper. The snowball is often psychologically stronger. The best method is the one you will stick to.

Be careful with high-cost borrowing

Some loans, especially quick-approval loan apps, payday-style loans and some store credit, can carry very high costs. Before borrowing, ask:

  • What is the total I will repay, not just the monthly amount?
  • What happens if I am late?
  • Is there a cheaper way to solve this?

Never borrow to pay for a lifestyle you cannot afford, and avoid borrowing from lenders who pressure you, hide fees or threaten you. If you are being harassed or threatened, keep records and seek help from the proper authority or consumer protection body in your country.

Talking to a lender

If you are struggling, contact your lender before you miss payments. Many are willing to discuss options. Rules and options vary by country and lender, and I am not a lawyer or financial adviser, so check local rules.

A script: "Hello, my name is [name] and my account number is [number]. I want to keep paying what I owe, but my situation has changed because [brief reason]. Could we discuss a revised payment plan or other options? I would like to find something I can realistically keep to."

Write down the date, the person's name and what was agreed.

Do not hide from it

The worst thing you can do with debt is avoid opening the letters. Facing it, even with a small plan, brings relief. A debt plan of "I will pay a little extra each month toward this one" is already a plan.

Borrowing from family and friends

Money lent between people you love can damage relationships. If you borrow, agree the amount, the repayment plan and the date in writing, even in a message, and keep to it. If you lend, only lend what you could bear never to see again.

Common Mistake 🚨 Common Mistake: Taking a new loan to pay an old one without understanding the total cost. This is how debt grows quietly.

12Where To Go To Learn And Earn More

A budget has two sides: spending less and earning more. Cutting costs has a floor, because you cannot reduce below your needs, but earning has a much higher ceiling. So let us talk about where to go to learn about money and to find extra income. You do not need to be everywhere. Choose two or three places that suit you.

A reminder: platforms, features and rules change often. Always check current platform rules before posting, messaging, selling or applying.

Your warm network

Your friends, family, former colleagues and neighbours are your most overlooked source of opportunities. Many people find their first extra income through someone they already know.

Script: "Hi [name], I am trying to build some extra income this year. I am good at [skill, for example organising, writing, cooking, tutoring] and I would love to help anyone who needs it. If you hear of anything, I would be so grateful for an introduction. Thank you!"

LinkedIn

LinkedIn is useful for professional growth, remote work and freelancing. Keep your profile clear, say what you do, and connect with people in fields you want to enter. Share small lessons you learn, and reach out politely to people who do work you admire.

Connection note: "Hi [name], I am working on growing my skills in [field] and I admire your work. I would love to connect and learn from your posts."

X (formerly Twitter)

X can be a place to learn from people sharing money and career lessons and to join short, helpful conversations. Follow trustworthy, educational voices and be cautious with anyone promising quick riches.

Facebook groups

Look for groups about personal finance in your country, women's business groups and local buy-and-sell communities. Read the rules first. Be careful: many "investment" and "money doubling" groups are scams, and anyone who sends you private messages offering to grow your money should be treated with deep suspicion.

Instagram, TikTok and Pinterest

These platforms have many money and budgeting creators. Use them for ideas, not as authority. Remember that people may be paid to promote products, and content is not personalised advice. Pinterest is especially good for visual budgeting templates and planner ideas. If you eventually want to earn by sharing what you know, these platforms can be places to build an audience slowly and honestly.

Reddit

Reddit has communities on personal finance, budgeting and careers. Read carefully, learn from experienced people and remember that advice varies by country. Never share personal financial identifiers or account details.

Marketplaces and job boards

Freelance marketplaces, job boards and local classifieds can connect you with extra income, from small services to remote roles. Complete your profile honestly, apply to roles that truly fit and check current platform rules and fees.

Local and in-person

Community boards, markets, local business owners, churches or mosques, schools and local events are all places to meet people who might need your skills. Printed flyers, word of mouth and kindness still work.

Cold messages and calls to earn more

When you reach out to someone you do not know, be respectful, brief and honest. Check local rules about unsolicited emails, messages and calls, and stop if someone asks you to.

Cold email to a small business:

Subject: Can I help with [specific thing] at [business name]?

"Hi [name], I noticed [specific, genuine observation]. I help small businesses with [skill], and I would be glad to do a small sample for you at no cost, so you can see if it is useful. No problem at all if now is not a good time. Thank you for your time. [Your name]"

Short call script: "Hello, may I speak with [name]? Hi, my name is [name]. I help local businesses with [skill], and I noticed [observation]. Would it be okay if I sent a short message with an idea? ... Thank you so much for your time."

Asking for a raise or better pay (to your employer):

"Hi [manager], I would like to schedule a short conversation about my role and compensation. Over the past [period], I have [two or three specific achievements]. I would like to discuss adjusting my pay to reflect this. When would be a good time to talk?"

Our free Salary Negotiation Calculator can help you prepare, and you can read more in How To Get Paid As A Freelancer.

Negotiating a bill:

"Hello, I have been a customer for [time]. I am reviewing my budget and I would like to know if there is a lower-cost plan or any discount available. Could you help me find the best option?"

You will be surprised how often a polite request lowers a bill. It costs nothing to ask.

13A Complete Plan To Earn More

Earlier I told you that spending less has a floor and earning has a higher ceiling. So let me give you a proper plan for earning more, step by step. I will not promise any figure, because your results depend on your skills, your market, your time and your effort. But I can give you a clear way to think.

The three levers of income

1. Earn more from what you already do. Ask for a raise, take on more responsibility, move to a better-paying role or improve the skills that decide your pay. 2. Add a side income. Use spare hours to sell a service, a product or your time. 3. Build assets over time. Create something that keeps earning, such as a digital product, a small business or, later, investments.

Lever one: earn more from your current work

Many people never ask for a raise, then wonder why their pay stays the same. Prepare properly:

  • Keep a wins list: a running note of what you achieved, with dates and, where possible, numbers.
  • Research what similar roles pay in your market, using several sources.
  • Choose a calm moment and ask directly, using the script earlier in this guide.
  • If the answer is no, ask what would need to change for a yes, and by when.

If your job truly cannot pay more, learning in-demand skills and moving to a better-paid role may be the long-term answer.

Lever two: a side income

A side income does not need to be impressive. It needs to be real, small and repeatable. Beginner-friendly ideas include:

  • Freelance services such as design, writing, virtual assistance, transcription or social media help
  • Tutoring or teaching a subject you know
  • Selling handmade goods or reselling items you can source fairly
  • Offering local services like cleaning, baking, braiding or event help
  • Selling simple digital products such as templates or planners

Pick one and test it for a month. Our guides can help you go deeper: How To Make Your First 1,000 Online and How To Get Your First Freelance Client.

Lever three: build assets slowly

An asset is something that puts money in your pocket or grows in value. Examples include a skill that keeps getting more valuable, an online product that sells repeatedly, a small business or long-term investments. Assets take time, so do not expect quick results.

Give your new income a plan before it arrives

This is where many people slip. Extra income arrives and instantly disappears into higher spending, a pattern called lifestyle creep. To prevent it:

  • Decide in advance what share of any new income goes to goals.
  • Raise your lifestyle slower than your income.
  • Keep enjoying the small, meaningful upgrades, but protect most of the increase.

A simple rule many people use: when you earn more, put half of the increase toward savings and goals and use the other half to enjoy life. You can adjust that to suit your situation.

Tax and legal basics for side income

I am not a tax adviser or lawyer. In many countries, extra income may need to be reported, and some activities need registration or licences. Rules differ widely and change. Please check what applies to you and keep clear records from the very first payment.

Track your side income separately

Keep a simple record with the date, who paid you, what for and how much. Open a separate account, if you can, so your business or side-income money does not mix with household spending. This makes budgeting and any future tax reporting far easier.

Reality Check 👀 Reality Check: Side income usually starts slowly. It is normal for the first month or two to bring little or nothing while you learn, test and find your first customers. Treat the early weeks as training, not as a verdict.

Take Halima, a made-up example, who works in an office. She spends two evenings a week offering simple social media help to local shops. In her first month she earns very little and spends most of it on a small tool subscription she did not need. She cancels the tool, keeps her prices fair and by month three has two regular clients. Her story is invented, and results vary a great deal, but the pattern of slow starts and small adjustments is realistic.

14Start Building Wealth: The Basics In Plain Language

I want to be careful and honest in this chapter. Investing and wealth building involve risk, laws differ by country and I am not a financial adviser. What I can do is explain the ideas so that you can ask good questions and make careful decisions, and so you can spot nonsense when you see it.

What "wealth" really means

Wealth is not a fancy car or a big house. At its simplest, wealth is how much freedom your money gives you. It is measured by your net worth: everything you own (savings, property, investments) minus everything you owe.

Wealth is built by a boring combination of things: earning, spending less than you earn, avoiding costly debt, protecting yourself and letting savings and investments grow over time.

The order that makes sense

For most people, a sensible order looks like this:

1. A starter emergency fund (small, quick). 2. Pay off costly, high-interest debt. 3. Build the emergency fund to a few months of needs. 4. Protect yourself with sensible insurance where available and appropriate. 5. Invest for the long term with money you will not need for many years.

You can do some of these in parallel. The point is not to invest before you have a safety net, because a surprise could force you to sell at a bad time.

Saving versus investing

  • Saving means keeping money safe and accessible. It is for short-term goals and emergencies.
  • Investing means putting money into things that can grow in value over time but can also go down. It is for long-term goals, typically many years away.

Never invest money you may need soon, and never invest money you cannot afford to lose.

Interest and compounding, explained simply

Interest is a payment for the use of money. If you save, a bank may pay you interest. If you borrow, you pay interest.

Compounding means your earnings also earn earnings. Imagine you save 100 and it earns 10 over a year. Next year, you earn on 110, not just on 100. Over a long time, the growth builds on itself, which is why starting early matters so much.

This example is only to illustrate how compounding works. It is not a prediction, and real returns vary and are never guaranteed.

Inflation, explained simply

Inflation is when prices rise over time, so each unit of money buys less. If your savings earn less than inflation, they slowly lose buying power. That is one reason people consider long-term investing for goals that are far away, while keeping their emergency fund safe.

Common types of investments (a plain-language overview)

I will describe these in general terms only. Availability, rules, taxes and risks differ by country, so please research your own options carefully.

TypeWhat it isGeneral risk idea
Savings accountsMoney held in a bank earning interestLower risk, lower growth
Fixed deposits or similarMoney locked for a set time at a set rateLower risk, limited access
Government or corporate bondsLending money to a government or companyVaries
Shares or stocksOwning small pieces of companiesHigher risk, higher potential
FundsA basket of many investments managed togetherSpreads risk, but not risk-free
PropertyLand or buildingsLarge, slow, needs care
Your own business or skillsInvesting in your ability to earnDepends on you and the market

Notice the last row. For many beginners, investing in your skills and income brings a better return than any financial product, because it raises the amount you can save in the first place.

Principles for beginners

  • Start small. You can learn a lot with a small amount.
  • Diversify. Do not put everything in one place.
  • Think long-term. Short-term ups and downs are normal.
  • Understand it before you buy it. If you cannot explain it simply, do not invest in it.
  • Keep costs low. Fees quietly reduce your returns.
  • Use regulated, reputable providers, and check your country's rules and protections.

Risk and honesty

All investments carry risk, including the possibility of losing money. No honest person can guarantee returns. If you are unsure, consider speaking with a qualified, licensed financial adviser in your country, and be clear about whether they are paid by commission.

Retirement and long-term security

Think about the longer future, too. Depending on your country, there may be pension schemes, retirement accounts or employer contributions. Check what you are entitled to and whether you are using it. Even small, regular contributions begun early can matter a great deal over decades.

Protecting what you build

  • Insurance can protect against large losses such as illness, accidents or damage. What is available and suitable varies by country and person, so research carefully and read the terms.
  • A will or plan for dependants may be worth considering as your life grows more complex. I am not a lawyer, so please check local rules.
  • Keep records of your accounts, loans and important documents in a safe place, and make sure someone you trust knows where they are.

A gentle wealth-building habit

Decide on a small, regular amount, even a modest one, to move toward your long-term goals each month, and automate it. Increase it whenever your income grows. The habit matters more than the amount at the beginning.

15Scam And Safety Warnings For Your Money

Because you are working hard to build something, scammers will want to take it. This chapter could save you a great deal of pain, so please read it slowly.

Common money scams

  • Money doubling or "guaranteed returns." Anyone promising to double your money, or guaranteeing profits, is lying. Real investments carry risk.
  • Ponzi and pyramid schemes. These pay early members using money from newer members and collapse when recruiting slows. If the main way to "earn" is by recruiting others, be very careful.
  • Fake investment platforms and trading groups. They show impressive screenshots and fake dashboards, then block withdrawals. Be wary of anyone who contacts you privately, uses urgency or shows off a lavish lifestyle as proof.
  • Romance and friendship scams. Someone you have met online builds trust and then needs money for an "emergency" or "investment."
  • Fake loan offers requiring upfront fees. A real lender does not ask you to pay a fee before releasing a loan.
  • Impersonation of banks and officials. Calls, texts or emails pretending to be your bank, asking for PINs, passwords or one-time codes. Real banks never ask for these.
  • Fake job offers asking you to pay. Real employers do not charge you to hire you.
  • Cheque and overpayment scams. Someone sends more than the agreed amount and asks you to return the difference. The original payment later fails.
  • Crypto and "signals" scams. Anyone selling guaranteed trading signals or promising easy crypto profits is not to be trusted. Digital assets are highly volatile and often involve scams.

How to protect yourself

  • Slow down. Scammers rely on urgency. A real opportunity will still be there tomorrow.
  • Verify independently. Look up the company yourself, check whether it is regulated in your country and call your bank using the number on your card, not the number in a message.
  • Never share passwords, PINs, one-time codes or full ID details.
  • Ask a trusted person before sending money to anyone new.
  • Be suspicious of secrecy. "Do not tell your family" is a red flag.
  • If it sounds too good to be true, it is.

If you have been scammed

Stop sending money, keep screenshots and records, contact your bank or payment provider immediately, change your passwords and report the incident to the relevant authority in your country. Please do not feel ashamed. Smart, careful people are targeted every day, and getting help quickly can make a real difference.

Big Sis Note 💖 Big Sis Note: The more urgent, secret and exciting an offer feels, the more slowly you should move.

16Four Worked Budgets For Different Lives

Budgets look different in different seasons of life. Here are four complete, made-up examples. The people and numbers are invented, for teaching only. Your numbers will be different, and that is completely fine. Read the one closest to your life and notice the shape of the plan.

Example one: the student with a small allowance

Take Efe, a made-up example, a university student who receives 60,000 a month from family and earns about 15,000 from occasional tutoring.

CategoryMonthly amountWhy
Food25,000Mostly self-prepared
Transport8,000Fixed routes
Data and phone6,000Essential for study
Study materials6,000Printing, books
Personal care5,000Basics
Fun and friends8,000Guilt-free
Savings goal (laptop)12,000Twelve months to buy one
Buffer5,000Small surprises
Total75,000

What to notice. Efe's savings goal is specific, and her fun money is protected. She tracks only two things weekly: food and fun. Everything else is nearly automatic.

Example two: the salaried woman supporting family

Take Ngozi, a made-up example, who earns 280,000 a month and sends money home every month.

CategoryMonthly amountWhy
Rent and utilities95,000Fixed
Food50,000Planned shopping
Transport25,000Commute
Data and phone8,000Needed for work
Family support30,000Planned and fixed
Debt repayment15,000Small loan
Personal care and clothes12,000Modest
Fun and treats12,000Guilt-free
Emergency fund20,000Building
Buffer and sinking funds13,000For known costs
Total280,000

What to notice. Family support is a fixed line, not a surprise. That makes it easier for Ngozi to give generously and to say, "I have already given what I planned this month."

Example three: the freelancer with irregular income

Take Tolu, a made-up example, a freelance writer whose monthly income ranges from 100,000 to 300,000. Her baseline is 130,000.

CategoryMonthly amountWhy
Needs (rent, food, transport, data)90,000Built on baseline
Tax set-aside12,000Kept separate
Fun and treats10,000Guilt-free
Emergency fund10,000Building
Business costs (tools, learning)8,000Needed
Baseline total130,000

In good months, Tolu allocates the extra: half to the buffer, a quarter to goals, a quarter to enjoy. In slow months, the buffer tops up her salary.

What to notice. Her plan runs on the lowest reliable number, so good months are a bonus, not a trap.

Example four: the couple sharing money

Take Kemi and Dayo, a made-up couple. They earn different amounts and want a fair, kind system.

Many couples use one of three setups:

  • Fully shared: all income goes into one pot and all costs come from it.
  • Fully separate: each pays their own costs and splits shared bills.
  • Hybrid: shared bills come from a joint account funded proportionally to each person's income, and each keeps personal money for their own choices.

Kemi and Dayo choose the hybrid method. They put a percentage of each of their incomes into a joint account for rent, food and shared goals. Each keeps a personal "no questions asked" amount. They hold a short money meeting once a month.

What to notice. Fairness is not always equal amounts. It is often equal proportions, with each person having some freedom. The monthly conversation matters more than the exact structure.

I am not a lawyer or financial adviser. Money arrangements in marriages and partnerships can have legal and tax implications that vary by country, so please check your local rules, especially around joint debts and property.

How to adapt these to your life

1. Pick the example closest to your situation. 2. Replace the numbers with your real ones. 3. Add any categories you need and delete those you do not. 4. Make sure the total of all lines equals your income. 5. Keep guilt-free spending in the plan. Every time.

17Talking About Money With The People In Your Life

Money conversations can feel awkward, but they are far easier than the problems that silence creates. Here are scripts for some common situations. Adapt the words to your own voice.

With a partner

"Hey love, I would like us to set aside twenty minutes this weekend to look at our money together. Not to blame anyone, just to make a plan we both feel good about. Would Saturday morning work?"

During the talk, begin with shared goals: "What do we want our life to look like in a year?" Then look at numbers. Speak about what happened, not about who is at fault.

With family who ask for money

"I love you and I want to help. This month I can give [amount]. I cannot do more right now because I am working on my own plan. I hope you understand."

Repeat it kindly as many times as you need to. Boundaries are not cruelty. They are what let you help sustainably.

With a friend about splitting costs

"I would love to join, and I am watching my budget this month. Could we pick something around [amount], or meet for a coffee instead?"

True friends will respect that. You will probably find that others feel the same and are relieved you said it.

With your landlord

"Hello, I have been a good tenant for [time] and I always pay on time. I would like to ask if there is any flexibility on the rent increase, or whether we could agree a payment schedule that works for both of us."

Check local tenancy rules before any negotiation, and keep the agreement in writing. I am not a lawyer, so check what protections apply where you live.

With a service provider or bank

"Hello, I would like to review my account and see if there are any lower fees or better plans that suit how I use it. Could you walk me through the options?"

When someone pressures you to spend or invest

"Thank you for thinking of me. I do not make financial decisions on the spot. I will think it over and look into it myself."

Anyone who gets angry when you say that is telling you something important.

Teaching children and younger siblings about money

If you are a parent, aunt or older sister, small lessons help: let them see you plan, give them a small amount to manage and let them make small mistakes safely. Money confidence, like any skill, is built by practice.

18Your Monthly Money Routine

A budget works best as a rhythm, not a one-time event. Here is a simple routine that takes very little time.

On payday (or when income arrives)

1. Move your fixed amounts first: savings, sinking funds, debt payments and bills. 2. Pay the essentials that are due. 3. Leave the rest in your spending account, with your guilt-free amount clearly separated.

Automating step one removes the need for willpower.

Every week (ten minutes)

  • Check your balance.
  • Update your spending.
  • See where you are in each category.
  • Decide one small adjustment.

At the end of the month (thirty minutes)

1. Review: what did I plan, and what actually happened? 2. Celebrate: write down one thing that went well. 3. Learn: which category was off, and why? 4. Adjust: change next month's plan based on what you learned. 5. Check goals: how close are you to each target?

Every quarter

  • Look at your net worth: what you own minus what you owe. Seeing it rise, even slowly, is motivating.
  • Review subscriptions and recurring costs.
  • Check whether your goals are still the right ones.

Every year

  • Review your income and ask whether it is time to earn more.
  • Look at your insurance, savings and long-term plans.
  • Set new goals for the year, with amounts and dates.
  • Review the way you use your retirement or long-term savings options.

A short routine, kept for years, beats a heroic plan abandoned in a month.

What to do when you go off track

You will have bad months: a surprise bill, a celebration, a hard season. Here is the recovery plan:

1. Do not panic or hide. Open your tools and look. 2. Find the cause. Was it a one-off or a pattern? 3. Adjust next month gently, rather than punishing yourself. 4. Restart the routine. Pick up where you left off.

Going off track is not the end of a budget. It is part of how a budget gets smarter.

Pause For A Second 🌸 Pause For A Second: Think of one money habit you already do well, even a small one. Maybe you pay bills on time, or you compare prices, or you never borrow. Notice it. You are not starting from nothing.

19Set Goals You Will Actually Reach

Goals give your budget a heartbeat. But the wrong kind of goal can make you feel worse. Let me teach you how to set ones that work.

Make them specific, measurable and dated

Weak goal: "Save more money." Strong goal: "Save 300,000 for an emergency fund by 31 December, by putting aside 25,000 each month."

A strong goal has four parts:

1. What you are saving or paying for 2. How much 3. By when 4. How you will do it (the monthly amount)

Use three time horizons

HorizonExamples
Short term (under one year)Starter emergency fund, a course, a phone repair fund
Medium term (one to five years)A laptop, a move, a wedding, school fees
Long term (five years plus)Home, business, retirement, financial independence

Work on one or two goals in each horizon at most, and give most attention to the short ones, because quick wins keep you moving.

Break big goals into small milestones

If a goal feels enormous, divide it into quarters and celebrate each one. A goal of 480,000 in a year can become four milestones of 120,000, each with a small, free celebration.

Connect each goal to a reason

Write one sentence about why the goal matters to you: "I want an emergency fund so I never have to borrow for a crisis again." On tired days, the reason is what keeps you going.

Review and adjust

Life changes. If a goal no longer fits, change it, without guilt. A goal is a tool, not a contract.

Playbook Note

Private — saved only in this browser.

20Category By Category: Practical Ways To Spend Smarter

Let me go through the main categories one by one, with simple, realistic ideas. You do not need to apply every idea. Pick one or two for each category that feel easy, and leave the rest.

Food

Food is often the most flexible big category.

  • Plan meals for the week, even loosely, so you shop with a list rather than hunger.
  • Cook in batches and use leftovers on purpose.
  • Compare prices at different markets or shops, and buy staples when they are cheaper, if you have space and the money to do so.
  • Notice delivery habits. Convenience has a price. Decide how many times a month you will use it and enjoy it on purpose.
  • Reduce waste. Using what you buy is the cheapest saving there is.

Transport

  • Check whether a different route, schedule or shared ride lowers the cost.
  • Group errands into fewer trips.
  • If you drive, remember the true cost includes fuel, repairs and parking. Maintenance saves money in the long run.

Data, phone and subscriptions

  • Choose the data plan that matches your real use, not the biggest one.
  • Download things on free Wi-Fi where possible.
  • Review subscriptions every quarter. Keep only what you truly use and enjoy.

Housing

  • Ask whether rent can be paid in a way that lowers the cost, such as an annual payment discount, though only if you can afford it without stress.
  • Reduce utility bills with simple habits like switching off appliances.
  • When your lease renews, ask politely whether the price can stay the same.

Clothes and personal care

  • Decide what you actually love wearing, and buy fewer, better pieces.
  • Wait twenty-four hours before non-essential purchases.
  • Sell or swap clothes you no longer wear, if you want to free up a little money.

Gifts and celebrations

  • Set a gift budget for the year and divide it among the people and events you know are coming.
  • Thoughtful, small gifts often mean more than expensive ones.
  • Plan your festive spending early with a sinking fund so it does not shock you.

Health

  • Keep up with check-ups and care. Neglecting health is expensive later.
  • Ask about generic or lower-cost options for routine needs, and speak with a qualified professional about what is suitable for you.

Learning and growth

  • This is one of the best places to spend. Skills increase your earning power.
  • Prefer free or low-cost learning first, and pay for a course when it clearly leads to income or a better job. Our free Academy and guides are a place to start.

Fun

  • Protect it. Choose a few things you truly love and spend on those.
  • Free pleasures count: walks, calls with friends, music, reading, time in nature.
Pro Tip 💡 Pro Tip: Pick just one category to improve this month. Small, sustained changes beat sweeping ones.

21A Net Worth Check-In: Your Money Scoreboard

Earlier I mentioned net worth. Let me teach you how to calculate it, because it is the single clearest picture of your money, and it moves in a satisfying direction when you follow a plan.

What net worth is

Net worth = everything you own minus everything you owe.

It is not about being rich. A person with a net worth below zero today, which is very common for people with student or other loans, can still be moving in a healthy direction. What matters is the trend.

How to calculate it, step by step

1. List what you own (assets): cash and savings, money in accounts, investments, the value of property or a vehicle you own, and money owed to you that you are confident will be paid. 2. List what you owe (liabilities): loans, credit, unpaid bills and borrowed money. 3. Subtract the second total from the first.

AssetsAmountLiabilitiesAmount
Savings and cashLoans
Emergency fundCredit or store accounts
InvestmentsMoney borrowed from people
Other valuablesOther debts
Total assetsTotal debts

Net worth = total assets minus total debts.

How often to check

Once every three months is plenty. Write the number in your notebook. Over a year, you will see a story: perhaps debts falling, savings growing, your emergency fund filling. That story is more motivating than any single month's budget.

A made-up example

Take Ada, a made-up example. In January she has 40,000 in savings and 180,000 in loans, so her net worth is minus 140,000. By December, she has built an emergency fund of 150,000 and reduced her loans to 110,000. Her net worth is now plus 40,000. She started the year below zero and finished above it. The numbers are invented, but the shape is real: steady, boring habits move the scoreboard.

Celebrate Yourself 🎉 Celebrate Yourself: The first time your net worth number goes up, even by a small amount, pause and mark the moment. That is evidence that your plan is working.

22A Leak Hunt: Find Your Hidden Money In One Evening

I promised earlier that I would show you a practical way to find leaks. Here is an evening exercise, with a cup of tea and your last two months of records.

Round one: recurring charges

Scan your records and list every charge that repeats. For each, write what it is, how much it costs, how often it is charged and whether you used it in the last month.

Ask three questions:

1. Do I use it? 2. Do I love it? 3. Would I buy it again today at this price?

If the answer is no to all three, cancel it. If it is a mix, consider downgrading.

Round two: the "little things" total

Go through your records for small, frequent purchases such as snacks, drinks, small transfers, airtime top-ups and tiny online orders. Add them all up for the month. Many people are surprised by the total. You are not trying to ban them. You are deciding whether that total matches what you value.

Round three: fees and charges

Look for bank fees, transfer charges, late fees, overdraft fees and withdrawal charges. These are often avoidable with small changes, like moving money in fewer, bigger transfers or paying bills before the due date.

Round four: the "unknown" line

Find every spend you cannot name. If it is large, it means you need tighter records for the next month. Starting tomorrow, write down every spend for thirty days, even small cash ones.

Round five: decide what to redirect

Add up what you found. Decide, in advance, where that money will go: perhaps half to your emergency fund and half to something you enjoy. If you do not give it a destination, it will leak somewhere else.

A made-up leak hunt

Take Bisi, a made-up example. She finds three subscriptions she barely uses, totalling 9,000 a month, and bank charges of 3,500 from many small transfers. She cancels two subscriptions and starts making fewer, larger transfers. That frees about 10,000 a month, which she sends to her emergency fund. Nothing painful was cut. She simply stopped paying for things she did not use.

23Planning A Whole Year: Sinking Funds In Practice

Now let us make your yearly costs predictable. This is one of the most freeing things you can do.

Step one: list the year's known costs

Go through the calendar month by month and write down anything you know will cost money:

MonthKnown costEstimate
JanuarySchool fees, new-year costs
MarchInsurance or annual subscriptions
MayBirthday or celebration
AugustBack to school, exam fees
OctoberPhone or laptop maintenance
DecemberFestive season, travel, gifts

Step two: add the total and divide by twelve

If your known yearly costs add up to 480,000, you need 40,000 a month in sinking funds. Put that into your plan as one line, or split into a few named pots.

Step three: save it monthly, in a separate place

When a cost arrives, pay it from the pot. If you do this for even one year, you will notice that "emergencies" shrink dramatically.

What if the total is too big?

Start with the largest or most stressful cost and fund that one first. Add others as your income allows. Or reduce the estimates: more modest festive gifts, a simpler celebration, or a cheaper option. Fund what you can, and grow from there.

A made-up example

Take Ruth, a made-up example, who always panicked in December. This year she lists her costs, finds that December alone costs 120,000, and saves 10,000 a month from January. In December, she paid everything from her pot, with no debt and no panic. She said it felt like receiving a gift from her past self.

24Common Mistakes (And How To Dodge Them)

Common Mistake 🚨 Common Mistake: Budgeting with guesses instead of real numbers. Fix: spend one to three months of records finding out what you truly spend.
Common Mistake 🚨 Common Mistake: Making the budget too strict. Fix: include guilt-free spending and a buffer from the start.
Common Mistake 🚨 Common Mistake: Having no emergency fund and relying on borrowing. Fix: start a tiny starter fund and automate it.
Common Mistake 🚨 Common Mistake: Forgetting irregular costs. Fix: create sinking funds for known yearly expenses.
Common Mistake 🚨 Common Mistake: Ignoring small leaks. Fix: review subscriptions and recurring charges every quarter.
Common Mistake 🚨 Common Mistake: Chasing investments before building a safety net. Fix: follow the order of starter fund, costly debt, bigger fund and then long-term investing.
Common Mistake 🚨 Common Mistake: Believing "get rich quick" promises. Fix: remember that guaranteed returns are a warning sign, not a feature.
Common Mistake 🚨 Common Mistake: Comparing your money to other people's social media. Fix: unfollow what makes you feel behind, and compare only with your own last month.
Common Mistake 🚨 Common Mistake: Quitting after one bad month. Fix: treat a bad month as data and adjust.
Common Mistake 🚨 Common Mistake: Keeping everything in one account. Fix: separate pots for bills, savings and spending protect you from yourself.
Common Mistake 🚨 Common Mistake: Lending more than you can afford to lose. Fix: only lend what you could bear never to see again.
Common Mistake 🚨 Common Mistake: Never increasing income. Fix: spend as much attention on earning more as on spending less.

25When Things Do Not Go To Plan: A Troubleshooting Table

The problemWhat it usually meansWhat to try
I run out of money before the end of the monthThe plan or timing is offMove bills closer to payday, shrink one category and check for leaks
I keep overspending on funThe guilt-free amount is too small or the habit is emotionalSet a realistic amount, use a separate pot and use the pause-and-ask technique
My income changes every monthIrregular incomeBudget on your lowest month and use a buffer account
I cannot save anythingNeeds are too high or income is too lowStart with a tiny automated amount, look at the biggest costs and work on earning more
I forget to trackThe tool is too hardSwitch to a simpler method such as a weekly check-in
I am drowning in debtToo many payments at onceList every debt, pay minimums and choose snowball or avalanche, and talk to lenders
My partner and I argue about moneyUnspoken expectationsHold a calm monthly meeting, start with shared goals and agree fair proportions
Family keeps asking for moneyNo boundariesCreate a fixed giving line and use the kind scripts
I feel guilty spending anythingMoney shame or scarcityRemind yourself that guilt-free spending is part of the plan
I got an unexpected billNo sinking fund or bufferUse your buffer, then add a sinking fund for next time
I lost motivationThe goals feel far awayBreak goals into small milestones and celebrate each one
I think I was scammedPossible fraudStop contact, keep records, call your bank using official numbers and report it

26Your Seven-Day Quick Start

If everything above feels like a lot, do just this for one week.

DayJobTime
1Write down your income for the last month15 minutes
2Write down your expenses for the last month30 minutes
3Sort them into needs, wants and savings20 minutes
4Choose a budgeting style15 minutes

6Set up a separate pot for your starter emergency fund20 minutes
7Do your first weekly money date10 minutes

After seven days, you have more clarity than most people ever have.

27Your Thirty-Day Plan

Week one: see clearly

  • Gather your records and find your real numbers.
  • Sort your spending into categories.
  • Find your biggest three costs and your biggest three leaks.

Week two: design your plan

  • Choose a budgeting style.
  • Set your needs total, your goals and your guilt-free amount.
  • Add a small buffer.

Week three: set up your system

  • Open separate pots or accounts where you can.
  • Automate your savings and bill payments.
  • Cancel one unused subscription.

Week four: live it and review

  • Follow your plan, with a weekly money date.
  • At the end of the week, review honestly and adjust.
  • Write down one win and one lesson.

28Your Ninety-Day Plan

MonthFocusGoal
Month oneLearn your numbers and set up your systemA written budget and automated savings
Month twoBuild your safety net and tackle costly debtA starter emergency fund and a debt plan
Month threeGrow your income and set long-term goalsOne income action and three written goals

At the end of month three, write a short note to yourself: what has changed, what has been hard and what you will do next. Then repeat, with slightly bigger goals.

29Mindset: The Voices That Show Up

"I earn too little to budget." Budgeting matters even more when money is tight, because every unit has to work harder.

"I will start when I earn more." Habits built now travel with you into every future income. Start small.

"Money is not spiritual or romantic." Money is a tool that protects the things you love, like peace, health, family and freedom.

"I am just bad with money." You are not bad with money. You were never taught. Skills can be learned at any age.

"Everyone else is doing better than me." You see people's highlights, not their debts. Compare only with your own past self.

"What if I fail again?" Then you learn and adjust. A budget that fails teaches you what to build next.

Coffee Break ☕ Coffee Break: If you ever feel overwhelmed, step away, make a cup of tea, and do just one small money action. One small action done is better than a big plan abandoned.

30A Month In Practice: Watching The System Run

Reading about a system is one thing. Seeing it run for a month is another. So let me walk you through one month, week by week, with a made-up woman called Sade (the same Sade from the structure earlier). Her numbers are invented, for teaching only.

Sade earns 250,000 and her plan is: needs 140,000, goals 45,000, extra debt 15,000, guilt-free 35,000 and buffer 15,000.

Payday

Her salary arrives on the 28th. Before she does anything else, she opens her banking app and moves money: 45,000 to her goals pots (split between an emergency fund and a laptop fund), 15,000 to a separate loan repayment, 15,000 to her buffer pot and 35,000 to her guilt-free spending account. Then she pays rent and sets aside the money for food and transport. She finishes in fifteen minutes and feels calm, because everything has a place.

Week one

She does her first weekly money date on a Sunday evening. She checks her food envelope and sees that she has spent a little more than planned. She decides to cook one extra meal at home next week. She notes it down and moves on, with no drama and no guilt.

Week two

A friend invites her to a restaurant. Sade checks her guilt-free account, sees there is plenty, and goes without feeling bad. She enjoys the evening fully. This is exactly why the guilt-free pot exists.

Week three

Her phone screen cracks. Repair costs 12,000. In an old life, this would have broken her month. Now she takes it from her buffer pot. She adjusts nothing else. The buffer did its job.

Week four

At the end of the month, Sade spends thirty minutes on her review. She finds that food ran about 5,000 over and transport ran 3,000 under. She decides to slightly move 3,000 from transport to food in next month's plan. She writes down one win: "I did not borrow when my phone broke." She also sees that her emergency fund is now at a quarter of her first target, and she marks that small milestone with a favourite meal at home.

What this shows

  • Nothing in the month was perfect, and the plan still worked.
  • The system handled both a treat and a surprise.
  • Total money time was about two hours for the whole month.
  • Sade felt in control, which is the real prize.

Your first month will probably feel clumsier, and that is fine. By the third month, the rhythm starts to feel natural.

Your own month: a simple template

Copy this into your notes and fill it in at the start of each month.

ItemMy planWhat actually happened
Income
Needs
Goals
Extra debt payments
Guilt-free spending
Buffer used
One win

Filling this in takes ten minutes and builds a record you will be glad to have in a year.

A word about patience

Money habits change slowly, then suddenly. The first few months can feel like a lot of effort for little visible change. Then one day you notice that you have an emergency fund, a smaller debt and a calmer mind. That day arrives for everyone who keeps going. Be patient with yourself, love. You are building a life, and that takes more than a month.

31Questions Girls Ask Me

How much should I save each month?

There is no single correct amount. A common starting guide is about ten to twenty percent of income, but if that feels impossible, start with whatever you can, even a small amount, and automate it. Increase it whenever your income or costs improve.

Should I save first or pay off debt first?

Many people build a small starter emergency fund first, so a surprise does not force more borrowing, then focus on costly high-interest debt, while paying minimums on everything. Your situation may differ, so consider talking to a qualified adviser.

What if I earn too little to save anything?

Start with a tiny, regular amount and look at your biggest costs for gentle trims. At the same time, work on earning more through a raise, a better role or a side income. Both sides matter.

How do I budget with irregular income?

Build your plan on your lowest reliable month, treat extra income as a bonus with set jobs and consider paying yourself a fixed monthly "salary" from a separate account.

Is it wrong to spend on fun?

No. A guilt-free spending amount makes your budget sustainable. A budget without joy is usually abandoned.

How big should my emergency fund be?

A common guideline is three to six months of essential expenses, built in stages. Start with a small, fixed amount, then one month of needs and grow from there. Irregular income or dependants may call for more.

Which is the best budgeting app?

The best one is the one you will open. Check that it suits your country, protects your data and has a free option. A notebook or simple spreadsheet works just as well.

Should I invest right now?

Many people first build a starter emergency fund and handle costly debt. Investing carries risk, laws differ by country and I am not a financial adviser, so learn the basics, start small and consider professional advice.

How do I avoid investment scams?

Be suspicious of guaranteed returns, urgency, secrecy and private messages from strangers. Verify any company with your country's regulator and never share passwords or codes.

How do I say no to family who ask for money?

Plan a fixed giving amount in your budget so that your answer is not about love but about limits. Say it kindly, as in the scripts above, and repeat it as often as you need to.

What if my partner and I handle money differently?

Start with shared goals, hold a calm monthly money meeting and agree on a fair setup, such as proportional contributions to shared costs with personal money for each person.

What do I do if I go off budget one month?

Do not panic. Review what happened, adjust next month's plan gently and restart your weekly money date. One off month is information, not failure.

33What To Do Next

You have just read a very long guide about something most people avoid, and that tells me you are ready to take care of yourself properly.

Here is what I want you to carry with you. A budget is not a punishment, a test or a lifelong sentence. It is a quiet, kind way of telling your money where to go, so that it serves the life you want. You do not have to be perfect. You do not have to be rich. You only have to look at your real numbers, make a simple plan, protect a little joy and keep showing up, week after week.

So here is your next step, and it is small. Tonight, write down what came in and what went out last month. Tomorrow, choose your budgeting style. By the end of the week, open a separate pot for your starter emergency fund and put a small amount in it. Keep it simple, keep it steady and be proud of every small step.

If you want to grow your income alongside your budget, How To Make Your First 1,000 Online and How To Get Your First Freelance Client are good next reads. And when you are ready to plan beyond a single stream, Build Your Online Empire will walk you through it.

I am rooting for you, babe. Take it one week at a time, and let your money follow your life.
